title: Eyelet stitch
subtitle: A pierced and overcast hole that forms the open spots and flower centres of broderie anglaise
excerpt: Eyelet stitch makes a clean round or oval hole in fabric by piercing the centre with a stiletto, then overcasting or buttonholing all around the edge to keep the hole open and neatly bound. It is the defining unit of broderie anglaise and appears as a standalone spot motif or grouped into flower and leaf shapes.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), broderie anglaise and eyelet chapters. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), eyelet and broderie anglaise entries.

content.text: An eyelet is a bound hole. The stiletto opens the hole by pushing the fabric threads aside rather than cutting them, which means the woven structure remains intact around the edge and holds the shape. The overcasting stitches that follow cover the raw edge and keep the hole from closing. In broderie anglaise, eyelets range from tiny round spots to elongated ovals and teardrop shapes; the same technique applies to all. A sharp embroidery needle is used for the overcasting, not a blunt tapestry needle, because the stitches must pierce the fabric close to the hole edge.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton 2 strands, or coton a broder no. 16; white on white fabric is traditional, but any single colour on a contrasting ground works

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Closely woven white cotton lawn or fine linen, 80 to 100 thread count; the tight weave holds the hole edge cleanly after piercing

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 8 or 9 for the overcasting; a stiletto or large-eyed awl for piercing the initial hole

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 15 cm hoop; fabric must be taut so the pierced hole stays open while you work around it

content.text: Mark the eyelet outline with a water-soluble pen or by tracing. For a round eyelet, mark a small circle. Secure the working thread on the back by running it under a few fabric threads near the eyelet. Bring the needle up on the marked outline.
Work a ring of small running stitches around the marked outline. These padding stitches raise the finished edge slightly and give the overcasting a firmer base.

Push the stiletto through the centre of the circle, rotating it gently to enlarge the hole to the required size. Work from the right side. The fabric threads should be pushed aside, not cut. For an oval or teardrop eyelet, work the stiletto in the direction of the long axis.

Overcast closely around the hole: bring the needle up through the hole from the back, then down into the fabric just outside the running stitch outline. Each stitch enters the hole and exits on the outside, covering the raw edge. Keep the stitches close together and at a consistent length so the edge is completely covered.

Continue overcasting all the way around until the starting point is reached. Take the thread to the back and fasten off under the worked stitches. On the right side, the hole should be clean and round with an even ridge of stitching forming the rim. Trim any loose threads from the back.

items.symptom: The hole closes up after the hoop is removed
items.cause: The fabric weave is too loose or the overcasting stitches were not worked close enough to the hole edge.
items.fix: Use a closely woven fabric and keep the overcasting stitches right at the hole edge, not several threads away from it. The stitches must physically hold the hole threads back.

items.symptom: The hole edge is ragged or has fraying threads
items.cause: The stiletto cut the fabric threads instead of pushing them aside, or the overcasting did not cover the edge fully.
items.fix: Rotate the stiletto slowly and steadily rather than stabbing. If fraying is visible, work the overcasting stitches slightly deeper to cover the frayed edge. On very fine fabric, a smaller hole is neater than a large one.

items.symptom: The overcasting stitches are uneven around the circle
items.cause: Stitch length or angle was varied as the needle turned around the curve.
items.fix: Aim to keep each stitch the same length and angled directly toward the hole centre. Working in good light makes it easier to see the hole edge clearly throughout.
